lesson.title: Checking Several Conditions Without Nesting
lesson.summary: The elif statement extends if-else to more than two possibilities, checking each condition in order and running only the first block whose condition is True, which keeps multi-way decisions flat and readable.
lesson.body:
An if-else statement handles exactly two possibilities: the condition is True, or it is not. Many real decisions have more than two outcomes, and the elif statement (short for "else if") is Python's way of handling that without stacking a new if-else inside the else block of the previous one. You can chain as many elif clauses as you need between the initial if and an optional final else, and Python checks them strictly in order from top to bottom, running the body of the first one whose condition turns out True and then skipping every clause after it, even if a later condition would also have been True.

That last detail, skip everything after the first match, is the part beginners most often get wrong, so trace it carefully with a grading example:

score = 85
if score >= 90:
    print("A")
elif score >= 80:
    print("B")
elif score >= 70:
    print("C")
else:
    print("F")

Python starts at the top. score >= 90 is False, since 85 is less than 90, so that block is skipped. Python moves to the first elif: score >= 80 is True, since 85 is at least 80, so it prints "B". Crucially, Python now skips every remaining clause, including elif score >= 70, even though 85 is also greater than or equal to 70 and that condition would independently have been True. The chain stops at the first match. This is exactly why the conditions here are ordered from most restrictive (90 and above) to least restrictive (70 and above): if the order were reversed, with score >= 70 checked first, then a score of 85 would incorrectly print "C" instead of "B", because 85 >= 70 is also True and would be matched first.

The elif statement builds directly on the if-else statement, keeping its core guarantee, that exactly one branch runs, while extending it from two branches to any number. Every condition in the chain is still just a boolean expression, so everything you know about logical operators and precedence applies equally inside an elif clause. The final else, if present, still serves as the catch-all default for whatever no earlier condition captured, exactly as it did in a plain if-else.

Compared to writing separate, independent if statements for each case, an elif chain is both more efficient and more correct: Python does not waste time evaluating later conditions once an earlier one has matched, and there is no risk of two unrelated if blocks both running when their conditions happen to overlap. When your conditions are mutually exclusive by construction, elif enforces that at the language level rather than leaving it to careful ordering of standalone ifs.

The ordering rule from the grading example generalizes into a habit worth keeping: whenever your elif conditions could overlap, such as several different threshold comparisons against the same variable, list them from most specific or most restrictive to least, so the first match Python finds is always the one you actually intended. If the conditions are mutually exclusive by their very nature, for example checking day == "Mon", then day == "Tue", and so on, order stops mattering, since no two of them could ever both be True for the same value at once.
